title: TypeLab
roles: Design and build, with Claude Code

cover.alt: TypeLab's letter editor in Points mode: a serif R drawn as an outline with its points

hero.alt: A one-minute screen recording: one font made in TypeLab, from picking a starting style to installing it on a laptop
hero.caption: I couldn't find the font in my head, so I built a tool to make it. In the video, I make one font, from picking a starting style to installing it on my laptop.

blocks.label: The problem
blocks.heading: Exploring type for a brand was painfully slow.
body: As a junior graphic designer on Clayco's Branding Experience team, I had a project that needed new letterforms. Drawing every idea by hand took days, and the fonts I downloaded only showed me what already existed.

image.alt: 1, Draw every idea by hand, days for each one: Illustrator at 734 percent on the lowercase g of my Didone specimen sheet, its 65 anchor points selected, beside the whole sheet with the g marked. 2, Collect fonts that exist, never the one in my head: six real typefaces printed as specimens and marked up by hand: Helvetica Neue Bold, too stiff; Didot, close, not quite; Impact, too loud; Snell Roundhand, too formal; Copperplate, almost?; Baskerville, seen it before

blocks.label: The idea
blocks.heading: Stack a few controls. Get a font no one else has.
body: TypeLab is an interactive font design playground: start from a style, reshape its proportions, shapes and details with plain-language controls, watch every letter update live, save designs to your library, and export a real .otf font.
55 controls in all, and every step redraws all 127 characters at once.

image.alt: TypeLab's editor, step by step on the word Galaxy in its Didone: 1, Weight from 64 to 90, Make strokes thicker; 2, Slant from 0 to 30, Tilt the letters; 3, x-height from 75 to 100, Make lowercase letters taller, with TypeLab's own x-height guides; 4, Stroke ends from Ball to Droplet, Choose how strokes end, the a's end magnified before and after. Each step shows the slider or tile changed and, marked with the same number, the part of the letters it changed, the step before faintly under the slant and the height

blocks.label: What you can do
blocks.heading: Experiment with type.
body: Every design starts from one of TypeLab's own fonts. Every setting reshapes their letters, and Points redraws any of them.

items.title: Start from 22 original typefaces.
items.caption: Free to change, use and share under the Open Font License, with filters by category and feeling.
items.alt: The Style page: starting typefaces as cards that read Design everything, under Sans Serif, with filters by category and feeling, each chip in its own typeface, and Customize at the foot

items.title: Reshape every letter with 55 controls.
items.caption: In three groups, proportions, shapes and details, each page named for what it does, like Make strokes thicker.
items.alt: The Weight page: Design letters in a Didone beside the panel Make strokes thicker, with Weight from Thin to Bold, and Verticals and Horizontals from Lighter to Heavier

items.title: Redraw any letter point by point.
items.caption: Its points (1); Only R (2), so an edit stays in this letter, where All letters sends it to every letter shaped the same there; and the construction grid it's drawn on (3), shared with its group.
items.alt: Points mode on the R of Headline Serif, with Only R and the construction grid on: the R's 35 points, the grid's lines and circles, those shared with its group in blue and its own in pink, under the note Only R changes here, weight, width and heights still move it; callout 1 on a point, 2 on Only R, 3 on the Construction grid switch

items.title: Add effects like halftone, pixels and rough print edges.
items.caption: Twelve fills, from wireframe to shadow, a slice, and rough edges.
items.alt: The Effects page: Change what fills the letters, with twelve fills, Solid, Wireframe, Pixels, Hexagons, Dots, Blobs, Liquid, Halftone, Lines, Inline, Outline and Shadow, then Slice and Rough edges

blocks.label: How I built it
blocks.heading: Built with AI in a month. The hard part: making it never break.
body: Most of the month was fixing things. Letters broke in ways I didn't see coming, so I had TypeLab test itself with 5,000 random setting mixes per round. I'd fix what broke and run it again. The first round found 149 broken designs. Now it's down to a handful.

Building with AI felt a lot like working with a developer. I learned to brief it clearly, give it specific feedback, and check every result with a designer's eye. That eye caught a lot of what the tests missed.

image.alt: A bar chart of broken designs found in each test round: 149 in round 1, then 19, 9, 2, 8, 1, 7, 4, 0, 1, 4 and 1 in round 12, and a handwritten note: …then I still checked every letter by eye

blocks.label: Usability test
blocks.heading: 13 problems found. 12 fixed two days later.
body: I worked through eight tasks as a first-time user would, in real Chrome, at 1440, 1024 and 390 pixels wide. Picking a style, changing it with sliders, saving and exporting a real font all worked. The biggest problems were about where things are, not whether they work. The three that blocked a task or lost work:
notes: The editor didn't fit screens narrower than about 1280 pixels, so Export was cut off on a laptop. Now the page list folds into a drawer below 1180 pixels, and Save and Export always show.
A name change was lost if you left without pressing Save. Now a rename takes effect at once, and leaving asks: Save and leave, Leave without saving, or Stay.
Everyone on the server shared one My designs list. Now each browser keeps its own, and an account keeps them on any computer.

images.alt: The usability test report's first page: 13 problems found, 3 high severity, 6 medium, 4 low, and all problems by severity
Problem 1 in the report: the editor doesn't fit screens narrower than about 1280 pixels

blocks.caption: From the test report, 2 October 2026: the 13 problems by severity, and problem 1 in detail.

blocks.label: Next
body: No real participants took part: the findings come from an expert walkthrough, so they show where people are likely to struggle. The next step is to test with three to five real users, such as typography students or designers new to type design.

title: Clack
statement: Ten satisfying materials to pop, squish and crunch with nothing but a cursor.

cover.alt: Clack's Cyanotype: white halftone dots exposed on cobalt blue where the cursor passed

hero.alt: Clack's website: the materials side by side, Cyanotype in the middle, with Play to start a sample agent under it

blocks.heading: Why
body: We pop bubble wrap, squeeze slime and watch soap get shaved into cubes, not to finish anything but because the small, repeatable feeling settles us. ASMR videos turned these textures into a genre, and on Roblox, ASMR tower obbies have players climb from one satisfying material to the next.
On a screen, though, we mostly watch. The textures are right there, but our hands never get to touch them. What if the cursor were the fingertip?

blocks.heading: The idea
body: The screen is laid out as a grid of invisible keys. Each cell the cursor crosses is pressed once: it plays a sound, and the picture under it reacts. Slow strokes tap, fast flicks sweep, and even an idle wiggle turns into a run of sound.
No clicks, no goals, no score to lose. Each sound draws its own picture, and the picture answers where you touch it: bubbles flatten, snow takes a boot print, soap gives up a path down to the paper.

blocks.alt: Five of the materials after a stroke of the cursor: Crunchy Slime, Cyanotype, Bubble Wrap, Wax Ball and Thocky Keys
blocks.caption: 01 to 05: Crunchy Slime, Cyanotype, Bubble Wrap, Wax Ball, Thocky Keys

blocks.alt: The other five materials after a stroke of the cursor: Chewy Jellies, Pudding, Soap Cutting, Squeaky Snow and Sugar Slime
blocks.caption: 06 to 10: Chewy Jellies, Pudding, Soap Cutting, Squeaky Snow, Sugar Slime

blocks.heading: Process
body: It started as a keyboard. The first version was called ddalkkak, the Korean word for a click: a full-screen keyboard that clicked under a passing cursor, with ten sound sets and seven keycap themes. The name clack comes from there.

Once the sounds turned into wax, slime and bubble wrap, a keycap was the wrong picture for them, so each sound got a picture of its own. Most ideas didn't survive being played: the lineup shrank to Bubble Wrap and Crunchy Slime, then grew back to ten. Seventeen materials were built, played and cut along the way.

blocks.heading: What broke
body: A quick stroke can fire twenty sounds a second, so anything with a hard edge (a ring, a ping, a thump) soon sounds like gunfire. Cyanotype went from a ringing twinkle to bubble blips to soft blips, and each still sounded like shooting under a fast cursor. Filtered noise with slow attacks fixed it, and became the recipe for the calmer sounds that followed.

blocks.heading: Result
body: Clack is on the Chrome Web Store as a browser extension. It opens in the side panel beside claude.ai or ChatGPT and wakes up as an answer starts. When the answer is done, the picture fades to gray and the sound stops: your cue to go back and read it.
It only checks whether the chat is writing an answer, by its stop button. It doesn't read your messages or the answers, and it sends nothing anywhere.

images.alt: Clack in the browser's side panel beside a chat, with the line Something to clack while your chat writes
When the answer is ready, the picture in the side panel fades to gray

body: At NBCUniversal, as a product design intern, I researched fashion, beauty, and lifestyle trends and transformed market insights into IP-based product concepts. title: Light Life

milestones.note: Lamp · business competition win, Temple University
Lamp and website redesign · graduation show, Sejong University

statement: Lighting designed to restore natural sleep rhythms.

cover.alt: Light Life poster: the name in a warm yellow glow on black

hero.alt: Two Light Life lamps stacked, lit white and warm yellow, on a yellow to blue gradient

blocks.heading: Context
body: Light Life is a lighting system designed to support sustainable, healthier sleep in environments that often disconnect us from natural light cycles. Many people struggle to wake up or wind down due to seasonal changes, jet lag, or limited daylight exposure. Light Life addresses this by recreating the rhythm of sunlight indoors, allowing users to experience gradual changes in brightness and color that feel familiar and intuitive rather than abrupt or artificial.

The system features a dual-sided design that separates ambient and functional lighting, allowing light to influence both space and behavior. By aligning light color, intensity, and direction with human circadian patterns, the design encourages improved sleep quality within everyday living spaces.

blocks.alt: Who it's for: people aged 18 to 35, patients, and parents

blocks.heading: The lamp
body: 2023: With it, my team won the Be Your Own Boss Bowl, a business competition at Temple University.
2024: I redesigned the lamp and its website for my graduation show at Sejong University. Link it to your time zone, flip it to stack the suns and expand the light, and rotate it to color your space.

blocks.alt: Three Light Life lamps, flipped and turned different ways, under the Light Life name
Two Light Life lamps side by side, each a rounded-square head with a white light over a ribbed base

blocks.heading: The app
body: 2026: I rebuilt its app: tell it your day and your city, and it suggests the light you need.
Like the lamp, each scene has two lights, each with its own job: white sunlight that shines on you, and a color that colors your space.

blocks.alt: The earlier Light Life app on a tablet, lying on a concrete surface
blocks.caption: The earlier app, on a tablet

blocks.heading: Reflection
body: From an object to a screen, it has grown the way I have.
